title: The Aim of Pleasing God
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: This sermon explores 2 Corinthians 5:6-11, focusing on the Christian's primary aim to please God in all things. The speaker examines how pleasing God is synonymous with doing all things for God's glory, and presents eleven characteristics of those who make pleasing God their central life ambition.

outline.title: The Aim of Pleasing God
subpoints: Paul's declaration in verse 9: 'we make it our aim, whether present or absent, to be well pleasing to him'
This aim encompasses both motivation and goal of the Christian life
To be well pleasing means to think, believe, and act in ways acceptable to the Lord
This theme is consistent throughout Paul's epistles

outline.title: The Connection Between Pleasing God and God's Glory
subpoints: Pleasing God is equivalent to doing all things for the glory of God
Glory (kabode in Hebrew, doxa in Greek) represents God's character, presence, and worthiness
Christ is the full manifestation of God's glory
Our actions declare either truth or lies about who God is through Christ

outline.title: Characteristic One: Recognizing Our Inability to Please God Apart from Christ
subpoints: No person can please God in and of themselves without faith in Christ
Believers must look to Christ's cross and resurrection, not inward, for assurance of God's pleasure
Unbelievers must first repent and turn to God in mercy

outline.title: Characteristic Two: Studying Scripture to Understand How to Please God
subpoints: We discover God's will through Scripture, worship, preaching, and fellowship with believers
The Psalmist delights to do God's will with His law in the heart

outline.title: Characteristics Three Through Eleven: The Life of a God Pleaser
subpoints: Conscious of pleasing God in all things; setting mind on things above
Motivated by love, not selfishness; understanding that love gives
Knows that giving is more blessed than receiving; others-oriented rather than self-centered
Focuses on what can be given, not what can be gotten; not consumed by fear or selfishness
Examines thoughts and motives behind actions, not just actions themselves
More concerned with God's view of the heart than man's view of appearance
Programs conscience by Scripture, not by culture
Does not avoid necessary confrontation or conflict when required
Does not worry about displeasing people if doing so pleases God

outline.title: Conclusion: Living for God's Glory
subpoints: The Christian life is a single all-encompassing ambition to please the Lord by displaying His glory
Every thought, choice, and action should declare the truth about who God is
We are created for His glory, redeemed by His Son, and called to be visible testimonies of His character
When God's character is reflected in us, we fulfill our purpose and proclaim His worthiness

transcript:
## Scripture Reading

> "For we are always confident, knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord. For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, yes, well pleased rather to be absent from the body and to be present with the Lord. Therefore, we make it our aim, whether present or absent, to be well pleasing to Him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ that each one may receive the things done in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad. Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are well known to God, and I also trust we are well known in your consciences." (2 Corinthians 5:6-11)

## Introduction: Goals and the Ultimate Aim

We are going to do something very unusual this morning. I want to ask you to raise your hand, not in worship, so do not be alarmed.

How many of you make goals? You can raise your hand. There you go.

How many of you always keep your goals? Sure. How many of you just lied?

Having goals in life is a helpful thing. It is good to have goals. It helps us to stay on track. It helps us to be efficient, to not be distracted by less important things. But goals are only helpful if they are the right goals for the season of life that we are in. The everyday goals for someone who is in the thick of raising little kids is going to be very different than the everyday goals for somebody raising teenagers. The everyday goals for a married person is going to be very different than the everyday goals for a single person.

Yet there is one goal that everybody in the world must make, even though non-Christians do not have the ability to fulfill it, and we do not have a choice to not keep it—we must aim to please God. This is what the Apostle Paul tells us in verse 9. The goal of all of our lives is to please God. Whether we are absent or present—and as we saw last week, this means whether we are alive or dead—we make our aim to please God. So we have this goal at all times in our lives. Every other season, we can do what we want, but in this life and the next, our goal must be to please God.

## Main Points

This morning we will consider three things: First, the aim of pleasing God itself. Second, the connection between pleasing God and doing all things for His glory. And third, the characteristics of the one who sets as his or her aim to please God. We will look at eleven characteristics of the God pleaser.

## Part One: The Aim of Pleasing God

### Understanding "Make It Our Aim"

Look at verse 9. Paul says:

> "Therefore, we make it our aim, whether present or absent, to be well pleasing to him." (2 Corinthians 5:9)

We read from the New King James as our pulpit version here. What the New King James has as "make it our aim" is literally "have it as our ambition," "have it as the innermost desire of our heart." It is stronger than a simple commitment to do something. It implies a whole-person purpose. It implies that the whole purpose of existing is to please God.

This is both the motivation and the goal of the Christian life. What motivates us as Christians is to please God. What pulls us and pushes us in life is that we want to please the Lord. If the goal and the motivation of life is to please Him, then we need to know who "him" is.

### Identifying Who We Please

If you look at verse 8, we have the word "Lord" there, which Paul normally uses for Jesus. But in verse 10, we have the word "Christ." So the one we desire to please is Christ. Our aim in life is to please Christ. Our motivation and our goal is to please Christ.

Paul says we make it our aim, whether present or absent, to be well pleasing to him. Now, the translation "well pleasing" is a bit redundant because there is no such thing as bad pleasing. All pleasing is by definition well pleasing. But that is what we are to do—we are to please Christ.

When we look at how this word is used in the New Testament, we realize that to make our aim to please the Lord is to think, to believe, and to act in ways that are acceptable to the Lord. This is a distinctive Pauline word. Paul uses it repeatedly throughout his epistles.

### Paul's Use of "Acceptable" or "Well Pleasing"

For example, in Romans 12:1-2, Paul says:

> "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies, a living sacrifice, holy, and acceptable or well pleasing to the Lord." (Romans 12:1-2)

In Romans 14:18, Paul says:

> "For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable or well pleasing to God and approved by man." (Romans 14:18)

In Ephesians 5:8-10, Paul says:

> "For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, finding out what is acceptable, again, well pleasing to the Lord." (Ephesians 5:8-10)

In Philippians 4:18:

> "Indeed I have all and abound. I am full, having received from Epaphroditus the things sent from you, a sweet-smelling aroma and acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God." (Philippians 4:18)

In Colossians 3:20:

> "Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well pleasing or acceptable to the Lord." (Colossians 3:20)

In Titus 2:9:

> "Exhort bond servants to be obedient to their own masters, to be well pleasing in all things, not answering back." (Titus 2:9)

So we can see that the thrust of Christian living is to be well pleasing to the Lord, to think, believe, and act in ways that are acceptable to the Lord. This is not the first time that Paul has shared this concept with the church in Corinth. The church in Corinth is the church that Paul wrote to the most. We have two canonical letters and there are two others that did not make the Bible, so Paul wrote at least four times to the Corinthians.

### The Equivalence: Pleasing God and God's Glory

In 1 Corinthians 10:31, Paul said:

> "Therefore, whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God." (1 Corinthians 10:31)

This is a synonymous and analogous way to what he says here in 2 Corinthians 5:9, where he says, "we make it our aim, whether present or absent, to be well pleasing to him."

To make our aim to please the Lord is the same thing as doing all things for the glory of God. That being the case, we need to figure out what this glory is, what is the glory of God that we are to do all things for.

## Part Two: The Glory of God

### The Meaning of God's Glory

In the Old Testament, glory generally represents the Hebrew word "kabode." The root idea is heaviness and gives the sense of weight or worthiness. So if we are to do all things to the glory of God, we are to do all things that are worthy of God, that display His worthiness to us.

The glory of God is often a synonym for who God is. When Moses asked God in Exodus 33:18, he said:

> "Lord, show me your glory." (Exodus 33:18)

God answers that question by showing Moses who He is by listing His attributes. In Exodus 34:5-6, the Lord answers that question. He says:

> "The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, abounding in goodness and truth, keeping mercy to thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sins, by no means clearing the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and the children's children to the third and the fourth generation." (Exodus 34:5-6)

Moses says, "Show me your glory." God says, "Here is my glory." And what does He show? Who He is. So the glory of God is who He is.

This is also implied in the vision that Isaiah had in Isaiah chapter 6. After seeing who God was, Isaiah thought he was going to die because of the statement in the Old Testament that you shall not see the glory of God and live. But what does Isaiah see in Isaiah 6? He sees who God is in his essence. And John in John chapter 12 tells us that the person sitting on the throne of the temple, when Isaiah saw it, was the Lord Jesus Christ himself. So Isaiah sees that the glory of God, even in the Old Testament, is seen in the face of the Lord Jesus Christ.

### The Temple and God's Presence

Eventually, the temple became the place where the glory of Yahweh was especially present. And what happened to Moses when he saw the glory of God? On his face he fell. What happened to Isaiah when he saw the glory of God? On his face he fell. And that trend continues. Every time somebody comes to know God, the first thing that happens is that they fall on their face, worshiping the God in complete and total dedication to the God whose glory they have just seen.

In 2 Chronicles 7:1-7, the chronicler says:

> "When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices. And the glory of the Lord filled the temple, and the priests could not enter the house of the Lord because the glory of the Lord had filled the Lord's house. When all the children of Israel saw how the fire came down and the glory of the Lord upon the temple, they bowed their faces to the ground on the pavement and worshiped and praised the Lord, saying, 'For He is good, for His mercy endures forever.'" (2 Chronicles 7:1-7)

When we see the glory of God through Christ, that is our reaction. We make our aim to declare that glory, to make that glory known, to show people how worthy our God is by the way that we act, believe, and think.

### The New Testament Understanding of Glory

When it comes to the New Testament, the New Testament borrows a way to speak about the glory of God that is found in the Old Testament's Greek translation. You may have noticed in your Bible that there is a little footnote, and the footnote says, "LXX says." The LXX is the Roman numeral 70, standing for the Old Testament Greek translation that was used by the time Christians arrived in the first century. In that translation, the Hebrew word "kavod" was often translated by the Greek word "doxa." You can hear the word "doxa" in "doxology," words of glory. A doxology is a little song, saying, or prayer that ascribes glory to God.

So in the New Testament, the word "doxa" is used. In certain places, it refers to the honor of man, but its chief use is to describe the revelation of the character and the presence of God in the person and work of Jesus Christ. So if you want to see the glory of God, you need to look at Jesus Christ. And if you make your aim to please Christ, you make your aim to do everything—whether you eat or drink, whatever you do—for the glory of Christ.

Christ is the outshining of the divine glory. There is this tremendous picture in the first chapter of the book of Hebrews. Starting in verse 1, the author of Hebrews says:

> "God who at various times and in various ways spoke in time past to the fathers by the prophets has in these last days spoken to us by His Son, whom He has appointed heir of all things through whom also He made the world, who being the brightness of His glory and the express image of His person." (Hebrews 1:1-3)

You want to know God? You need to know Jesus. You want to see God? You need to see Jesus. You want to please God? You can only do that through Jesus Christ because He is the incarnation of God's glory.

### The Fall and Redemption Through Christ

Man, who was made in the image of God and for relationship with God to declare His glory, has fallen short of what He was created for. We all have sinned and we fall short of the glory of God, which has been fulfilled only in Christ, the second Adam. He fulfilled the glory of God.

In Hebrews 2, the author of Hebrews says:

> "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor." (Hebrews 2)

Brothers and sisters, the objective of the church is this: we exist to see that the world acknowledges the glory that is God's and is shown in His deeds, in His disciples, and above all, in His Son, the Lord of glory. That is our aim in life.

### Pleasing God Through Our Relationships

In Romans 15:7, Paul says:

> "Receive one another just as Christ also received us to the glory of God. Now I say that Jesus Christ has become a servant to the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers and that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercies." (Romans 15:7)

Did you see there? Paul says that as we relate to one another as believers, if we do it the way that God calls us to do, the Gentiles are going to see the glory of God. People outside of the church are going to see the glory of God, much like what Jesus said in John 17.

So when we are cranky with one another, when we behave as if we do not love each other, we are defaming the glory of God in the world. And that is very important. That is why reconciliation in the church of Jesus Christ is so important. If you make your aim to please Christ, you are also making your aim to reconcile relationships in your life. If you refuse to do so, you are not acting as a follower of Jesus Christ. And you have great reason to look in your heart and see if you are truly redeemed.

If you are willing to have a bad relationship with your husband, with your wife, if you are willing to have a bad relationship with your children, if you are willing to not do whatever is possible in your power to live at peace with all people, you are not making your aim to please Christ. And perhaps you have never been redeemed. Because Paul says—Jesus says—that one of the ways we proclaim the glory of God to Gentiles is by the way that we relate to one another.

### Christ as the Revelation of God's Glory

Ultimately, the glory of God is fully displayed in Jesus Christ, who is the only way to know the character and the presence of God. In John 1:14, the evangelist says:

> "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And what was it that we beheld? We beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." (John 1:14)

### What It Means to Do All Things for God's Glory

So what does it mean when the Bible tells us to do things for the glory of God? Well, we already saw that it is the same thing as making our aim to please God, but it adds a little bit to the meaning.

We have also seen that the glory of God is the weight of His presence and His character manifested. So to do things for the glory of God is to do things in such a way that God's character and presence are displayed.

Did you get that? Say it again, there is some distraction going on here. To do things for the glory of God is to do things in such a way that God's character and presence are displayed.

And if we are not doing that, we are not aiming to please Christ. We do not add glory to Christ when we do things for His glory because He is from all eternity perfect without any need of addition. We declare His presence and who He truly is when we do things for His glory. And this word "truly" is very important in this statement because by our baptism, by our profession of faith, by our membership in the local church, we have declared ourselves to be part of the body of Christ. We declare Christ to be our head and the body to be His. We have said, "Christ is my head and what I am doing is His doing through me."

So everything we do is a statement of whom God in Christ is. Do you get that? If you are professing, baptized, and believing in the Lord Jesus Christ, a member of a local church, everything you do is you saying, "That is Christ doing that, because the body does not act apart from the head."

The problem is that we may be lying about Christ, right? And when we do things that are not aimed to please Him, we are doing just that. We are declaring lies about our Savior. And that is a very dangerous thing to do. But when we do things for His glory, then we declare things that are true about Him. And this is done with or without words.

### The Principle Extended to All of Life

We can even broaden the principle here. So Paul says:

> "Therefore, whether you eat or drink, and then there is that pesky word—whatever you do, do it for the glory of God." (1 Corinthians 10:31)

When we eat, drink, or do whatever else we do, the idea that we exist to declare the character and presence of God governs us. No matter what that is. As you leave and go have a cup of coffee, you are going to do that for the glory of God. How does that look? That is something you are going to have to figure out.

From the simplest, most mundane act of basic life—eating and drinking—to the most complex or non-essential acts of life, the fact that God is real and that Christ is our Lord must be evident in what we do.

So to make our aim to please God is to commit to doing all things for the glory of God.

## Part Three: Characteristics of the God Pleaser

What kind of person does that? Well, let me give you eleven characteristics of a person who makes his or her aim to please God. I will try to be brief on this.

### One: Recognizing the Inability to Please God Apart from Christ

The first one is the most important one. So if you do not get any others, get this one. The God pleaser realizes that he or she cannot please God apart from faith in Christ. The Bible makes it emphatically clear that no person is capable of pleasing God in and of himself or herself without Christ.

Romans 8:8 does not take a lot of exegesis, does not take any knowledge of Greek language. Paul says:

> "So then, those who are in the flesh cannot please God." (Romans 8:8)

That is it. So if you are not in Christ, you will not please God. You just will not. You cannot. There is nothing you can do in and of yourself that is going to please God.

Proverbs says that God hates the wicked. Proverbs says that even the plowing of the wicked is an abomination. So the only thing that will please God, if you are an unbeliever, is for you to turn to Him, beat on your breast, and say, "Be merciful to me, a sinner."

A recognition that you cannot please God is where you need to begin. For those of you who are believers but are looking for reasons why God is pleased with you in your heart, stop it. You are not going to find any. It is not by looking within that you are going to find that God is pleased with you. It is by looking at the cross of Christ and the empty tomb, the one who rose from the dead, who lives to reign and bless His church. That is how you are going to find that you please God.

So if you are trying to look down and find reasons why God has accepted you in your heart, stop. Look to Christ. That is where the pleasure is. That is where the one is who has done all things.

### Two: Studying Scripture

Number two: The God pleaser studies the scriptures to understand exactly what it takes to please God. We do not go look at the trees. We do not go on a camping trip. We do not go anywhere else. No, we look at the scriptures and figure out how to please God. We come and worship Him. We hear God's word preached. We fellowship with God's people. That is how we know how to please God.

Again, Paul says, in Ephesians 5:8-10:

> "For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, finding out what is acceptable to the Lord." (Ephesians 5:8-10)

The Psalmist says in Psalm 40:8:

> "I delight to do Your will, O my God, and Your law is within my heart." (Psalm 40:8)

You want to know what pleases God? Look in the Bible, not somewhere else.

### Three: Consciousness of Pleasing God

Thirdly, in everything he or she does, the God pleaser is conscious of pleasing God. Colossians 3 starts with the word "if," but that should be the word "since." It is not a condition; it is a true-to-fact conditional sentence.

> "Since then you were raised with Christ, seek those things which are above where Christ is, sitting on the right hand of God. Set your mind on things above, not on things on the earth." (Colossians 3:1)

So if your life is full of anxiety and you struggle in doing what God calls you to do, ask yourself: how is your thought life? If you are spending fifty hours a week playing video games, watching TV, on Instagram, on TikTok, or whatever other things are in social media that I do not know about, and you are really struggling, well, let us start by setting your mind on things above. That is a good way to start. And the rest of life follows.

### Four: Motivated by Love, Not Selfishness

Four: When he or she pleases people, the God pleaser does so out of loving motives, not selfish ones. The God pleaser knows that love is giving, because that is how God loves us.

> "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son." (John 3:16)

As Paul says:

> "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave Himself for me." (Galatians 2:20)

And:

> "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her." (Ephesians 5:25)

Loving is giving.

### Five: Others-Oriented, Not Self-Centered

Five: The God pleaser knows that it is more blessed to give than to receive. So the God pleaser is not self-centered but others-oriented. Is your life about you? Then you are not making your aim to please Christ.

> "It is more blessed to give than to receive." (Acts 20:35)

### Six: Focused on What Can Be Given

Six: Because the person who loves to please God is not consumed by selfishness or fear, his or her focus is on what he or she can give, not on what he or she can get. Are your broken relationships because you are always judging people, thinking they have not given you what you think you deserve from them? You are not making your aim to please God because as Paul says:

> "Love does not behave rudely, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil." (1 Corinthians 13:4-5)

### Seven: Examines Motives and Thoughts

Seven: He or she considers changing not only his actions but also his thoughts and motives. Why am I doing what I am doing? That is a question we need to ask because it is out of a good heart that a good tree produces good fruit, as in Luke 6:45.

> "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and an evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things." (Luke 6:45)

### Eight: God's View of the Heart, Not Man's Appearance

Eight: He or she is more concerned with what God sees in his heart than what man sees in his appearance. Remember when Samuel came to anoint David? He went to Bethlehem, came to Jesse. Jesse had kids, yes. The first one comes in, strong and tall and fit, and Samuel says, "Yes, that is the king. Just look at him. Nobody can deny." And God says, "Nope. Remember why? God says to Samuel, 'Man looks on the outward appearance, but I, God, look at the heart.'" (1 Samuel 16:7)

### Nine: Programs Conscience by Scripture, Not Culture

Nine: He or she, the God pleaser, programs his or her conscience by the Bible rather than by culture. What bugs you is what bugs God. What pleases you is what pleases God. Hebrews 10 says that in Christ, by the Spirit, you have been cleansed from an evil conscience. So you do not go by the whims of culture but by what the scriptures say.

> "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water." (Hebrews 10:22)

### Ten: Does Not Avoid Necessary Confrontation

Ten: He or she does not shy away from necessary confrontation or conflicts. A God pleaser will not shy away from necessary confrontation or conference. Proverbs 28:23 says:

> "He who rebukes a man will find more favor afterward than he who flatters with the tongue." (Proverbs 28:23)

### Eleven: Not Concerned With Displeasing People for God

And eleven: The God pleaser does not worry when he or she displeases people if by doing so they please God. Do you get that? Because our ultimate satisfaction is not that people be pleased with us, but that God be pleased, because we make our aim to please Him.

All these characteristics are present in the one who makes his or her aim to please God.

## Conclusion

In the end, the Christian life is not a collection of disconnected duties but a single all-encompassing ambition to please the Lord by displaying His glory in everything we do. From the smallest, most ordinary acts like eating or drinking to the most significant decisions we face, our lives are meant to declare the truth about who God is as revealed in Jesus Christ.

We were created for His glory, redeemed by His Son, and now we live as visible testimonies of His character in the world. Therefore, let every thought, every choice, every action be governed by this aim—not the pursuit of self, not the assertion of our rights, but the humble, joyful pursuit of making God known.

For when His character is truly reflected in us, when His holiness, His mercy, and His love are seen in how we live, then we are fulfilling our purpose, pleasing our Lord, and proclaiming with our lives that He alone is worthy of all glory.

Therefore, Paul says, make your aim to please the Lord. We make our aim, whether present or absent, to be well pleasing to Him. My glorious God, we know that on our own we cannot please You, but we thank You that the Lord Jesus Christ has already pleased You, and now we aim to align our lives with what You require of us. Give us grace to do so. We pray that all of us will set as our aim in life to please Him who has pleased You, for we ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.
